extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of patent applications to determine patentability under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112, including claim interpretation, prior art searching, and preparation of Office actions. Primarily directed to USPTO examiners but also used by applicants/agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution / Complete first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action; deficiencies should be explained clearly, particularly when they serve as a basis for a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever practicable, examiners should indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. Where a rejection not based on prior art is proper (lack of adequate written description, enablement, or utility, etc.) such rejection should be stated with a full development of the reasons rather than by a mere conclusion. Failure to follow this approach can lead to unnecessary delays in prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what invention is sought
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to focusing on statutory requirements, examiners must determine what precisely the inventor or joint inventor has invented and is seeking to patent, and how the claims relate to and define that invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners will review the complete specification, including the detailed description, any specific embodiments disclosed, the claims, and any specific, substantial, and credible utilities. After understanding the invention, the examiner will conduct a prior art search and then determine statutory compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and understand any asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention as a whole must be useful; examiners should review the application to identify any asserted utility or practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete disclosure should contain some indication of the practical application for the claimed invention (e.g., why the applicant asserts the invention is useful). Regardless of form, the utility statement must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the applicant asserts the claimed invention is useful. The application may describe more than one utility; only one is necessary. Alternatively, applicant may rely on contemporaneous art for a well-established utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the written description to exemplify the invention, explain how it relates to the prior art, and explain the relative significance of various features of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should (A) determine the function of the invention (what it does when used as disclosed) and (B) determine the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application. Correlate claim limitations to portions of the disclosure that describe them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim analysis: analyze each limitation and correlate to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the property rights provided by a patent and require careful scrutiny; examiners should identify and evaluate each claim limitation and correlate each limitation to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For processes, limitations define steps; for products, discrete structures or materials. Correlate limitation to all portions of disclosure that describe it, regardless of means- or step-plus-function language. Consider the claim as a whole (do not dissect), and give claim terms their plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP §§2111 et seq. for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the supporting disclosure during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammar and plain meaning generally dictate claim scope. Positive limitations from the specification cannot be read into a claim that does not itself impose that limitation. Give means- or step-plus-function limitations their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with all corresponding structures/materials/acts described in the specification and their equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language types that may raise questions as to limiting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim language may raise questions whether it is limiting: (A) statements of intended use or field of use (preamble), (B) 'adapted to'/'adapted for' clauses, (C) 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, (D) contingent limitations, (E) printed matter, (F) terms with associated functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether particular language is a limitation depends on the specific facts of the case. See MPEP §§2111.02–2111.05 for how to determine limiting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a thorough search of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to evaluating patentability, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of the prior art, including both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search should take into account structure/materials described in the specification and their equivalents corresponding to means- (or step-) plus-function limitations in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§2181–2186. See MPEP §§904–904.03 for search procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (Patentable Subject Matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and whether the claim is directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two criteria: (a) claim must fall within a statutory category; (b) claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception (see Alice framework). Avoid focusing solely on 35 U.S.C. 101 to the detriment of 102/103/112 analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101: Four requirements interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 has been interpreted as imposing four requirements: (i) only one patent may be obtained for an invention (no double patenting), (ii) inventors must be identified appropriately, (iii) claimed invention must be eligible for patenting, and (iv) claimed invention must be useful (utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2104 for discussion. Each requirement must be evaluated as part of the patentability determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 requires that only one patent may be obtained for an invention; identical subject matter claimed in more than one application to same inventive entity leads to statutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 8.30, 8.31, 8.32 for statutory double patenting rejections. See MPEP §804 for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of inventor / inventorship correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor(s) must be the applicant (for applications filed before Sept. 16, 2012) or must be identified in applications filed on/after that date; incorrect inventorship can lead to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101/115 or pre-AIA 102(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rare cases where application clearly does not name correct inventorship and applicant has not filed correction under 37 CFR 1.48, examiner should reject claims accordingly. See MPEP §2109 and §602.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) / Definiteness and 'particularly point out and distinctly claim'
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) requires claims to set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention and to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; indefiniteness is judged in light of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is deficient under 112(b) if evidence outside the application shows the inventor regards the invention as different from what is claimed. Claims must set out and define the invention with reasonable precision and particularity; claims, interpreted in light of the disclosure, must reasonably apprise a person of ordinary skill of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific 112(b) topics (new terminology, ranges, functional/alternative limitations, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific topics that commonly raise 35 U.S.C. 112(b) issues include new terminology, relative terminology, numerical ranges and amounts, exemplary claim language ('for example', 'such as'), lack of antecedent basis, reference to limitations in another claim, functional limitations, alternative limitations, negative limitations, product-by-process claims, 'use' claims, omnibus claims, reference to figures/tables, chemical formulas, trademarks in a claim, mere function of a machine, prolixity, multiplicity, double inclusion, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§2173 et seq. and related subsections for examination and form paragraphs. Breadth is not indefiniteness per se; analyze in view of specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether the disclosure provides support for the claimed subject matter. Consider typical circumstances where written description issues arise, burden on examiner, relationship to new matter, and how changes to scope of claims impact written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation; the specification must be enabling as of the filing date and enabling to persons skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider quantity of experimentation, working and prophetic examples, predictability of the art, burden on the examiner, examples of enablement issues in biological, chemical, and computer programming cases, and that enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims. See MPEP §§2159–2164 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining compliance with the best mode requirement requires a two-prong inquiry: (1) did the inventor possess a best mode at the time of filing; and (2) if so, does the written description disclose the best mode so that one of ordinary skill could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deficiencies related to best mode are rarely encountered during examination because evidence to support such deficiencies is seldom in the record. See MPEP §2165 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) and analogous treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation may be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even if it does not use the word 'means' when it uses a generic placeholder coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure; conversely, 'means' or 'step' may not invoke 112(f) if sufficient structure/materials/acts are recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 112(f) applies, the limitation is interpreted to cover the corresponding structure/materials/acts described in the specification and equivalents. Use the three-prong test in MPEP §2181. Provide form paragraph rejections where disclosure of corresponding structure is lacking, or where it's unclear whether 112(f) applies. Applicant may amend claims or clarify the record; mere assertions of intent are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty / anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review claimed invention against prior art; if no differences exist between the claimed invention and prior art, the claim lacks novelty and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what constitutes prior art (printed publications, patents, public use, on sale, foreign/domestic applications), the date of availability, level of public accessibility, admissions as prior art, and whether references are enabling. See MPEP §§2126–2160 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying differences between the claimed invention and prior art, assess whether those differences render the claimed invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate level of ordinary skill, legal concept of prima facie obviousness, suggestion or motivation to modify references, reasonable expectation of success (is required), consideration of all claim limitations, implicit disclosure, reliance on scientific theory or common knowledge, secondary considerations (objective indicia), and obviousness of ranges/species. See MPEP §§2141–2146 and related subsections. Use appropriate form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and bases; use form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing a rejection, ensure a prima facie case of unpatentability exists; Office actions should clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and the reasons which support them, and examiners should use applicable form paragraphs to state the basis for objections or rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using form paragraphs reduces misunderstanding as to grounds of objection or rejection. Review all proposed rejections and their bases prior to issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution laches and res judicata (procedural grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history laches may forfeit applicant's right to a patent in egregious cases of unreasonable and undue delay; res judicata may preclude seeking claims not patentably distinct from claims finally refused or canceled in a prior adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laches applies only in egregious cases and examiner should obtain TC Director approval before making such a rejection. Res judicata rejections should be applied only when the earlier decision was final (PTAB or court) with no opportunity for further review; base rejections on same prior art where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.130) and exceptions to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome prior art rejections by showing inventor-originated disclosures, earlier public disclosures by inventor, or derivation by another who obtained subject matter from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes who may file an affidavit/declaration, situations where they are unavailable, showing that disclosure was made by inventor or by another who obtained material from inventor, and related procedures. Also consider joint research agreements and other statutory exceptions under the AIA.
